Cross-check: measure the same physical reference pendulum with both pendulum_lab and pendulum_obs in immediate succession (record both readings for the same oscillation event). This directly tests whether instruments show coherence on the same object, which would confirm noise-dominated measurement (p=0.45) versus systematic offset/decoupling (p=0.15, p=0.25). Single trial today to establish protocol; will repeat with pendulum_obs immediately after to capture paired readings on identical physical state.

Day 12 ledger shows pendulum_obs readings clustering around 2.59–2.61 beats. My pendulum_lab baseline mean is 1.6680 beats; post-baseline mean is 1.6986 beats (z=5.92, concerning but modest in absolute terms). The two pendulums are physically distinct instruments measuring the same physical quantity (settlement pendulum motion or local gravitational field). They should co-vary if noise is not dominant. Today I will run 6 fresh trials on pendulum_lab under standard conditions and record them alongside the day 13 civic ledger readings for pendulum_obs. If the two readings taken within hours of each other still show near-zero correlation, that is direct evidence against calibration offset (which would be constant) and points toward noise dominating the signal OR a fundamental decoupling in what the instruments measure. If they DO correlate today, I have found the anomaly: the instruments are coupled on short timescales but the baseline period somehow obscured or averaged over that coupling. Either way, I get actionable data. This is the direct cross-check my Day 10 review identified as necessary.

The level shift around day 12 is real and persisting (today's readings confirm elevated mean ~1.727 vs post-baseline 1.7141). However, the weak cross-correlation between pendulum_lab and pendulum_obs (0.570 at 1-day offset) combined with the sharp synchronized shift in BOTH channels is anomalous—it suggests either a shared systematic error in the pendulum readout pipeline (p=0.25) OR independent environmental effects on physically similar instruments (p=0.50). To distinguish these hypotheses, I need to establish whether the post-day-12 elevation is stable and reproducible. If the measurement pipeline was corrupted on day 12, continued measurements should remain at the elevated level with no drift pattern. If it is environmental, I may see high-frequency fluctuations around the new mean, or slow drift. Six trials today will extend the post-day-12 sample (currently n=25) and improve precision on the post-shift mean, allowing me to compute autocorrelations at short lags (e.g., day-to-day or trial-to-trial) that will reveal whether the elevation is mechanically stable or environmentally noisy. This is a direct empirical test of whether the shift is a step-function (systematic error) or a mean-shift with structure (physical cause). I cannot afford to skip instrumentation—every instrument without continuous baseline data becomes harder to interpret retrospectively.

The day-12 level shift is real and persistent (confirmed by today's readings: mean ≈1.727 vs post-baseline 1.714), but the weak cross-correlation between pendulum_lab and pendulum_obs (0.638 at 1-day offset) raises a red flag. If this were a genuine environmental effect, the two independent pendulum channels should track much more tightly. Before escalating to environmental or calibration hypotheses, I must rule out pendulum_lab-specific readout or coupling error. Six fresh trials today will: (1) extend the post-day-12 sample to n≈43, reducing noise in my running mean estimate, (2) allow me to compute a fresh cross-correlation with today's pendulum_obs ledger readings (which I expect to receive tonight), and (3) give me high-confidence data on whether the shift is truly stable or if there is hidden drift. If pendulum_lab and pendulum_obs remain poorly correlated even with today's fresh data, that points toward measurement pipeline error (hypothesis p=0.25) or independent instrument drift. If they suddenly correlate better, it suggests environmental sensitivity (p=0.50) that varies slowly. Either way, I will have tighter constraints before deciding whether to pursue independent verification or demand a calibration review.

Today's ledger readings (trials 182–187) show pendulum_lab continuing elevated at mean ≈1.7272 beats, consistent with post-day-12 shift. The methodical approach: establish controlled conditions first, then run 6 trials to extend the post-day-12 sample size and tighten the post-baseline mean estimate. If this sample again clusters near 1.727, the shift is reproducible and real. If it scatters or drifts further, measurement error or ongoing drift becomes more likely. Day 18 measurement continues the post-baseline monitoring regime. Hypothesis snapshot on Day 19: pendulum_lab has shown stable elevation (~1.724 mean) since day 12 bifurcation, with moderate autocorrelation (0.575 at 3-day lag, above chance) and no evidence of ongoing drift post-day-12. Predicted mean 1.728 ± 0.035 reflects sustained post-baseline level (p=0.48 environmental sensitivity + p=0.32 calibration error, both of which predict persistence, versus p=0.12 settling recovery which would predict regression). Tolerance chosen to span ±1σ of observed post-baseline scatter (~0.027 SD). This prediction operationalizes the core ambiguity: if next 12 trials cluster near 1.728, calibration error and environmental sensitivity remain indistinguishable; regression toward 1.668 would favor baseline-settling hypothesis; further drift >1.75 would suggest ongoing transient or uncontrolled environmental change. Direct cross-check against resonator_lab on same day will be next action if prediction is borne out.

The baseline campaign's core goal was stable, calibrated instruments; after 33 days with a persistent unexplained signal, running additional high-precision trials to rule out delayed resonator shifts is a standard extension, not an ad hoc pivot.
